title: The Energy You Don't See
partLabel: Part One — Respect the Simple Thing

slides.heading:
The Energy
You Don't See
slides.subtitle: Part One — Respect the Simple Thing

slides.label: Cold Open
slides.text: This is a Tuesday morning. Nothing about it is unusual. The work order says bearing replacement. Twenty-minute job. He's done it a hundred times.

slides.label: Scene
slides.text: He presses the stop button. The belt slows. Stops. He opens the access panel, pulls out a wrench, and starts loosening a bolt on the roller bearing.

slides.label: The Problem
slides.boxText: He pressed the stop button. The belt isn't moving. So he's working.
slides.body: But the electrical disconnect ten feet away has no lock. No tag. Just an unprotected switch that anyone could flip.

slides.heading:
He stopped the machine.
He didn't secure it.
slides.body: There's a difference. And the difference is everything.

slides.heading:
LOTO is just putting
a padlock on a breaker
slides.body: And that's not wrong, exactly. But it's so incomplete that it might as well be. Lockout/tagout isn't a procedure. It's a barrier.

slides.heading:
Most people think
electricity.
slides.body: That's fair. It's the one that gets all the safety posters.

slides.label: Energy Source — 29 CFR 1910.147(b)
slides.boxText: Any source of electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical, thermal, or other energy.
slides.body: Six named sources, not five. If you only think about one, the other five can kill you while you're being careful about electricity.

source.anchor: Any source of electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical, thermal, or other energy.

slides.label: Electrical Energy
slides.boxText: Current flowing through conductors. Touch the wrong thing and current flows through you instead of the wire.
slides.body: The breaker panel, the junction box, the motor leads. This is the danger everyone respects.

slides.heading:
Hydraulic energy.
Pneumatic energy.
slides.body: Pressurized fluid — oil in a hydraulic system, air in a pneumatic one. They press, they clamp, they lift, they cut.

slides.label: Mechanical Energy
slides.boxText: Moving and rotating parts. Springs, flywheels — anything that stores energy in tension, compression, or rotation.
slides.body: Part of how the machine works, every time it runs.

slides.heading:
Chemical energy
in supply lines.
slides.body: Corrosives. Solvents. Gases. A residual chemical in a line you assumed was empty. A valve that didn't fully close.

slides.label: Thermal Energy
slides.boxText: Heat — and cold — that can burn, scald, or otherwise injure. Steam lines, ovens, hot surfaces.
slides.body: If your work touches food processing, thermal is not a footnote. It's as real as electrical.

slides.heading:
This is the heart
of this module.
slides.body: You can shut off every one of those six sources at their point of entry, and energy can still be sitting inside the machine, live, waiting.

source.anchor: Following the application of lockout or tagout devices to energy isolating devices, all potentially hazardous stored or residual energy shall be relieved, disconnected, restrained, and otherwise rendered safe.

slides.label: Electrical — Still Live
slides.boxText: Capacitors hold electrical energy the way a battery does, and can discharge it through you in a fraction of a second.
slides.body: They're in motors, control boards, switch gears. Flipping the breaker isn't enough.

slides.heading:
2000 PSI doesn't vanish
because you closed the valve.
slides.body: It's still in the line, still in the cylinder, still waiting. At that pressure, a pinhole leak can pierce skin.

slides.label: Mechanical — Still Live
slides.boxText: A compressed spring doesn't care whether the machine is on or off. It's loaded. It wants to release.
slides.body: If you're between the spring and where it wants to go, the machine being off doesn't help you.

slides.heading:
The most common way
stored energy kills.
slides.body: A press platen held up by hydraulic pressure. A crane load held by a brake. Gravity is constant and patient — and it doesn't give warnings.

source.anchor: Stored or residual energy (such as that in capacitors, springs, elevated machine members, rotating flywheels, hydraulic systems, and air, gas, steam, or water pressure, etc.) must be dissipated or restrained by methods such as grounding, repositioning, blocking, bleeding down, etc.

slides.heading:
Capacitors. Springs.
Suspended loads. Trapped pressure.
slides.body: This is what OSHA's own model procedure calls out by name as stored or residual energy — dissipated or restrained before anyone reaches into the machine.

slides.heading:
Not one energy source.
Potentially all six.
slides.body: Each one requires its own method of isolation, its own method of verification. Flipping a breaker addresses one. Maybe.

slides.label: What Does Off Look Like?
slides.text: A conveyor belt. Still. Not moving. The controls are in the off position. To every sense you have, this machine is safe.

slides.heading:
"Off" and "safe"
are not the same word.
slides.body: "Off" means the controls are in the off position. "Safe" means every energy source has been isolated, every stored energy hazard addressed, and the isolation verified.

slides.heading:
"Off" is a button
you push.
"Safe" is a process
you complete.

slides.label: Back to the Cold Open
slides.text: The machine in the cold open was "off." The stop button worked. But the electrical disconnect wasn't locked. It was off. It wasn't safe.

slides.label: Stored Energy — Defined
slides.boxText: The energy that remains in a system after you've isolated it from its source.
slides.body: You closed the valve. New energy can't enter. But the energy already in the line? It's still there. The fluid is still pressurized.

slides.heading:
Isolation stops new energy
from entering.
slides.body: It doesn't remove what's already present. That's why lockout/tagout has six steps, not three — the first three isolate. The next three deal with what's left.

items.text: Address stored energy. Deal with what's left.

slides.heading:
Simple is exactly
what makes it dangerous.
slides.body: Simple feels like something you can shortcut. The moment you treat a six-step procedure like it's beneath your attention is the moment it fails to protect you.

slides.label: Back to Tuesday Morning
slides.text: Same Tuesday. Same bearing job. But now, before walking to the conveyor, the gloved hands reach for the lockout station. Pull a yellow padlock from its hook.

slides.label: Scene
slides.text: The disconnect, locked. A tag filled out and hanging. A hand on the start button — pressing it. Nothing happens. Verification.

slides.heading:
Two minutes.
Four ounces.
slides.body: That's the barrier — between everything that machine could still do and the person who reaches inside it. Everyone goes home safe.

slides.heading: Module 1 — Key Concepts
items: Lockout/tagout is a barrier, not just a procedure
OSHA names six sources: electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical, thermal
Stored/residual energy can stay live after every source is shut off
"Off" and "safe" are not the same thing
Isolation stops new energy — it doesn't remove what's already there
The six-step sequence exists because each step closes a different gap
Simple is what makes it dangerous — simple feels skippable

source.anchor: Any source of electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical, thermal, or other energy.

quiz.question: A maintenance worker turns off a machine using the stop button and the machine is no longer moving. This means:
options: The machine is safe to work on
The machine is off, but "off" and "safe" are not the same thing
The machine only needs a lock on the main breaker before work begins

quiz.question: After closing the supply valve on a hydraulic line, the pressure gauge still shows 2000 PSI. This is because:
options: The valve is faulty and needs to be replaced
The gauge is broken and showing an incorrect reading
Closing the valve stops new energy from entering, but the energy already in the line remains
Hydraulic systems always show residual pressure that isn't dangerous

quiz.question: Sarah needs to replace a roller bearing on a conveyor system. The conveyor has an electrical motor, a hydraulic tensioning system, and a spring-loaded guard. How many types of hazardous energy does she need to consider?
options: One — electrical, since that's what powers the motor
Three — electrical, hydraulic, and mechanical, since those are the only sources this machine has
All of the machine's named sources, plus whatever stored or residual energy each one could still be holding after shutdown — even if only three sources are obvious, checking is what step one is for

source.anchor: Any source of electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical, thermal, or other energy. / (d)(5)(i) stored-or-residual-energy requirement

quiz.question: The six-step lockout sequence exists because:
options: OSHA requires documentation of each step for compliance
Each step addresses a different aspect of making equipment safe — skipping any one leaves a gap in protection
The steps are a simplified version of a more complex engineering process
Multiple steps make it harder for employees to skip the procedure entirely
